title: Sausalito from the N.P.C.R.R. Wharf, Looking South
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Purchase, The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Gift, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 1991
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A photograph in brown and gray tones looking across a wharf toward the town of Sausalito, with water, ships, and a few men.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, credit line, classification, tags (Men, Rivers, Ships), public-domain flag, and image URLs read from the record. Region is a well-established label for Sausalito, California, not a record field.

context: A photograph by Eadweard Muybridge made around 1868, looking from a wharf toward Sausalito, California. Before his famous studies of motion, Muybridge worked as a landscape and city photographer in California.

descriptions.k: This old photograph shows a town by the water. There are ships and a wharf. A few men are there too. It is brown and gray. What do you think the ships carry? Can you find a person?
descriptions.g12: Eadweard Muybridge took this photograph of the town of Sausalito, California, from a long wharf. You can see water and ships. A few men are in the picture. It was made more than 150 years ago, so it is brown and gray. What might be happening on the wharf?
descriptions.g35: Before Eadweard Muybridge became famous for photographing horses in motion, he photographed places in California. In this picture from about 1868, he stood on a wharf and looked toward the town of Sausalito. The title tells the direction: looking south. Look for the ships, the water, and the people. What does this photograph tell you about life by the bay long ago?
descriptions.g68: This view of Sausalito from a wharf shows Muybridge working as a landscape and documentary photographer around 1868, years before his motion studies. The title records exactly where he stood and which way he faced, a habit of survey-style photography. The glass negative and albumen print capture the fine detail of ships, water, and people. Look at how the wharf pulls your eye into the scene. What does the picture reveal about work and travel on the water?
descriptions.g910: Sausalito from the N.P.C.R.R. Wharf, Looking South belongs to Muybridge's early California work, long before his motion studies. The long title behaves like a surveyor's note, fixing viewpoint and direction, and the albumen print records ships, water, and men with a documentary clarity. Consider how the composition uses the wharf and water to create depth, and how photographs of growing towns also served commerce and local pride, a purpose the record itself does not state.
descriptions.g1112: Made around 1868, this photograph shows Muybridge as a documentary and landscape photographer in a rapidly changing California. Its title, with an abbreviation for a company and a compass direction, reads like a field note and situates the image within commercial and civic uses of photography. Printed as an albumen silver print from a glass negative, it captures harbor life with notable clarity. We can ask what the photograph was for, who might have bought it, and whom it leaves out, questions the Met record alone cannot answer.

k.daily: Imagine you are standing on this wharf. What sounds do you hear?
k.emotion: Does this harbor feel busy or sleepy to you? What do you see that tells you?
k.observation: Find a ship, some water, and a person. Where are they?
k.analysis: What does your eye notice first in this old photograph?
k.line: Find a long straight line, like the edge of the wharf. Where does it lead you?
k.shape: What shapes do the ships make? Look for tall ones and flat ones.
k.color: This photograph is brown and gray. Why do you think old photographs look this way?
k.texture: How do you think the wooden wharf would feel under your feet?
k.space: What is closest to you in this harbor picture and what is far across the water?
k.light: Do you think it is morning, noon, or evening here? What tells you?
k.meaning: Why do you think someone wanted a photograph of this town and its ships?
k.culture: Long ago, ships brought goods to towns by the water. How do goods get to your town today?
k.technique: The photographer used a heavy camera and glass. Why do you think he stood on the wharf?
k.personal: Have you ever watched boats or ships come and go? What was it like?
k.critical: The photograph shows only the view in one direction. What might be behind the photographer?

g12.daily: What do you think life was like in Sausalito when this photograph was made? Use details to explain.

g12.observation: List four things you see, from the wharf to the far side of the water.
g12.analysis: How does the wharf lead your eye into the picture?
g12.line: Follow the long lines of the wharf and the water's edge. Where do they take you?
g12.shape: The ships and buildings make different shapes. Which shapes are tall and which are low?
g12.color: The picture has soft browns and grays. How do they make the scene feel old?
g12.texture: Which parts look smooth, like water, and which look rough, like wood?
g12.space: How can you tell which parts of the harbor are close and which are far?
g12.light: Where does light fall on the water or ships? What does it make you think of?
g12.meaning: Why might a photographer stand on a wharf to photograph a whole town?
g12.culture: Harbors were important for travel and trade in California then. Why might ships matter to a town?
g12.technique: Photographers in the 1860s carried glass plates and chemicals. Why would that be hard on a wharf?
g12.personal: What would you want to see on a wharf like this? What would you want to do?
g12.critical: The title tells you the direction the photographer faced. Why might that be useful?

g35.daily: What clues in the photograph show the activities and the setting of this California harbor town?
g35.emotion: What mood does the water and wharf scene create, and which details lead you to it?
g35.observation: Take one minute of silent looking. What small details about the ships, water, or people stand out?
g35.analysis: How does Muybridge organize the wharf, water, ships, and town so your eye travels through the picture?
g35.line: How do the long lines of the wharf and the horizon give structure to the photograph?
g35.shape: How do the tall shapes of masts or ships contrast with the flat shape of the water?
g35.color: An albumen print has warm brown tones. How do they affect the way you see the scene?
g35.texture: How does the photograph let you tell the difference between wood, water, and ships?
g35.space: What clues in the photograph, such as size and overlapping, show how far away the town is?
g35.light: How does the light on the water help you understand the weather or time of day?
g35.meaning: The title is long and exact. What does it tell you about why the photograph was made?
g35.culture: How were ships and wharves important to life and work in California towns around 1868?
g35.technique: Muybridge made this with a glass negative. How would that be different from taking a quick snapshot today?
g35.personal: Think of a place you know with water or a harbor. What view would you choose to photograph?
g35.critical: A photograph of a town may be used to show it off. How might that change what the photographer chooses to include?

g68.observation: List what you see from the foreground wharf to the distant shore. Which details do you only notice on a second look?

g68.texture: How does the sharpness of the print help you read the textures of wood, rigging, and water?
g68.space: How do overlapping forms and tonal change create a sense of distance across the bay?
g68.light: How does light on the water create contrast with the dark forms of ships?
g68.meaning: What does the exact wording of the title suggest about the picture's purpose?
g68.culture: How were ports like Sausalito changing in the 1860s, and how might photographs reflect that?
g68.technique: What challenges would a photographer face working with wet chemicals and glass plates on a wharf?

g1112.emotion: How does the photograph's sober clarity shape an emotional register that differs from picturesque landscape?
g1112.observation: Describe the print's formal construction precisely. Which observations depend on assumptions about the harbor or the date?
g1112.analysis: Analyze how Muybridge's viewpoint and framing produce an image that is both informational and compositionally resolved.
g1112.line: How do linear structures such as the wharf and horizon create a framework for reading space?
g1112.shape: How does the interplay of man-made forms and natural water produce visual tension?
g1112.color: How does the tonality of an albumen print mediate between document and image?
g1112.texture: How does the level of detail in the print contribute to its credibility as evidence?
g1112.space: How does the print position the viewer physically and socially in relation to the town?
g1112.light: How does light function in the print as a record of a specific moment and a constructed effect?
g1112.meaning: How does this early work complicate the narrative that Muybridge's career began with motion studies?
g1112.culture: How do images of developing ports participate in narratives of progress and settlement in the American West, and what do they omit?
g1112.technique: How do the limits of early photographic technology shape the ways people appear, or fail to appear, in views like this?
g1112.personal: How does your familiarity with present-day photography shape your assumptions about what the image is documenting?

teacherNote.context: Eadweard Muybridge is best known for his motion studies of the late 1870s, but he also photographed California landscapes and towns. The Met record dates this view ca. 1868; the initials in the title are given as they appear in the record.
directions: Have students write a precise title for a photo of the school that tells where the photographer stood and which way they faced.
Ask students to compare this view with a modern photo of a harbor and list what has changed.
Discuss how photographs of towns can serve both as records and as advertisements.
